#9703. The NVIDIA Controversy Exposes a Bigger Vulnerability in America's AI Strategy

Anastasios (Tasos) Tassos — GM at 7projectsAI & BCLA, Founder of GeopoliticsOfAI.com, MBA Lecturer & PhD(c) in IR

Anastasios (Tasos) Tassos — GM at 7projectsAI & BCLA, Founder of GeopoliticsOfAI.com, MBA Lecturer & PhD(c) in IR

Anastasios (Tasos) Tassos — GM at 7projectsAI & BCLA, Founder of GeopoliticsOfAI.com, MBA Lecturer & PhD(c) in IR

What the NVIDIA controversy reveals about private power, national AI capability and the governance of strategic dependence

The controversy surrounding NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is easy to read as a story about personal conduct, corporate governance and alleged Chinese intelligence activity. That reading is incomplete.

The more consequential question is structural. What happens when a state's ability to convert artificial-intelligence resources into national capability depends heavily on a privately controlled corporate chokepoint whose leadership, commercial networks and security practices remain only partially subject to state control?

That question matters regardless of how the current investigation concludes.

On 8 November, NVIDIA's board announced an independent investigation following reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, supported by outside counsel, will oversee the inquiry. The board stated that it currently has no reason to believe either US national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised. Huang separately acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife and said he would cooperate with the investigation.

Those are established facts. Other elements remain allegations or intelligence assessments reported by major media organisations. US officials reportedly believe that Alice Huang, an executive associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed International, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and cultivated access to Jensen Huang. Singapore has explicitly rejected reports that its own authorities investigated Alice Huang for alleged intelligence ties, while confirming that investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing.

The distinction is essential. The public evidence does not establish that Alice Huang obtained NVIDIA trade secrets, that sensitive US information was passed to China, or that Jensen Huang altered company policy at the direction of a foreign actor. Any analysis that assumes those conclusions would be premature.

Yet the episode is already strategically revealing because it exposes a vulnerability that exists before any successful espionage is proved.

NVIDIA occupies an unusual position in the emerging AI political economy. Its importance derives not simply from market capitalisation or technological sophistication, but from where it sits in the conversion of AI resources into usable capability.

Advanced accelerators are required to train and operate many frontier systems. NVIDIA's hardware, networking products, software ecosystem and developer tools help determine who can assemble large-scale AI infrastructure, at what cost and on what timetable. Governments attempting to control China's access to frontier compute have therefore relied heavily on restrictions affecting NVIDIA products.

This makes NVIDIA a corporate chokepoint.

A chokepoint is strategically significant when access to a concentrated resource or infrastructure can enable, mediate or constrain the capabilities of others. NVIDIA does all three. Its products enable AI development. Its allocation decisions, technical ecosystem and relationships with cloud providers mediate access. Export restrictions on its most advanced hardware are used by the United States to constrain the capability conversion of a strategic competitor.

The central point is that this strategic leverage is privately organised.

Washington can impose export controls, investigate diversion and set national-security rules. It does not, however, manage NVIDIA's customer relationships, executive networks, commercial incentives or day-to-day information flows. The state therefore depends on a private organisation to produce a resource that has become strategically indispensable while retaining only partial control over the organisation through which that resource is governed.

That is a form of privately mediated power.

Most discussion of technological chokepoints focuses on leverage. If one actor controls a critical node that others cannot easily substitute, that actor gains power.

The more indispensable the node becomes, the more consequential its internal vulnerabilities become as well.

A concentrated chokepoint reduces substitutability. That is precisely why it is valuable. But low substitutability also means that governance failure, coercion, penetration, policy divergence or leadership exposure at the node can produce effects far beyond the company itself.

NVIDIA illustrates this logic particularly clearly. A foreign intelligence service interested in the future trajectory of advanced AI would not necessarily need the source code of a GPU design to gain strategically valuable information. Access to senior decision-makers could, in principle, provide insight into demand, product roadmaps, customer priorities, expected export-control changes, supply constraints or the company's political calculations regarding China.

This does not mean such information was obtained in the present case. It shows why the leadership network around a corporate chokepoint becomes a rational intelligence target.

The same concentration that gives the United States leverage over access to advanced compute can therefore create concentrated exposure.

This suggests a candidate mechanism that may be described as chokepoint inversion: the conditions that make a corporate node strategically powerful can also magnify the consequences of failures in its governance.

The proposition should remain provisional. It requires comparative testing across other strategic firms and sectors. But the NVIDIA episode makes the mechanism visible.

The Geopolitics of AI capability-conversion framework distinguishes technological capacity from national capability.

A country may possess firms, capital, advanced chips, research institutions and data centres without being able to convert those resources reliably into strategic effect. Conversion takes place across three linked layers: Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation. Governance operates across all three.

At the Invention layer, the company sits close to the technological frontier and has unusually deep visibility into the direction of model development and compute demand. The strategic issue is not only protection of proprietary designs, but also control over anticipatory knowledge: which architectures, customers and workloads are likely to become important next.

At the Industrialisation layer, NVIDIA is one of the principal mechanisms through which AI capability is scaled. Its accelerators, systems and software ecosystem shape the physical build-out of AI capacity. US export controls attempt to use this chokepoint to slow China's access to the most advanced computing infrastructure.

At the Operationalisation layer, the problem becomes more difficult. The physical location of a chip does not necessarily determine who receives its computational value. A restricted processor may remain in a data centre outside China while Chinese users access compute remotely. Cloud delivery, intermediaries, resellers and offshore infrastructure can therefore separate hardware geography from capability geography.

This is why scrutiny of firms such as Megaspeed matters beyond any allegation involving an individual executive.

Singapore has confirmed that investigations into Megaspeed continue. Bloomberg has separately reported that NVIDIA is strengthening location monitoring for accelerators sold in Southeast Asia, requiring customers seeking NVIDIA Cloud Partner status to participate in a fleet-intelligence system that can provide data on accelerator location and other metrics. The timing does not prove that the new controls are a direct response to the Megaspeed controversy. It does show that physical control and end-use verification are becoming part of AI industrial strategy.

The broader lesson is that export control is no longer only a border problem. It is an operational-governance problem.

The episode also exposes a distinction that becomes increasingly important as governments build industrial strategies around national champions.

A company can be globally dominant, headquartered in a country and central to that country's strategic advantage without being fully integrated into national capability.

National-capability integration requires more than ownership location. It depends on the extent to which private capacity can be aligned with public strategic objectives while remaining secure, reliable and available under pressure.

For a corporate chokepoint such as NVIDIA, this includes at least five conditions: effective protection of sensitive information, credible export-compliance systems, resilience against foreign influence and penetration, reliable state-firm information sharing, and sufficient alignment between corporate incentives and national-security requirements.

Weakness in any of these areas does not turn the firm into an adversary. It creates a gap between corporate capacity and national capability.

That gap is where strategic vulnerability emerges.

The United States can benefit enormously from NVIDIA's technological leadership while simultaneously confronting risks created by the fact that NVIDIA is a private global corporation with customers, executives and commercial interests that cross geopolitical boundaries.

This is not an anomaly. It is likely to become a defining feature of AI power.

The immediate policy response will understandably focus on counter-intelligence, executive security and board oversight. Congress has already moved in that direction. The chairs of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Select Committee on China and the House Intelligence Committee have requested a closed-door briefing from Huang on his interactions with Alice Huang and on NVIDIA's safeguards against foreign-adversary espionage.

Those questions are necessary, but the underlying governance problem is broader.

The issue is whether states have developed institutions capable of governing privately controlled infrastructures that have become part of national strategic capability.

Traditional corporate governance asks whether directors protect shareholders, manage conflicts and supervise executive conduct. National-security governance asks additional questions. Which executives are exposed to foreign influence? Which customer relationships create strategic risk? Who can access sensitive roadmaps? How are unusual procurement patterns investigated? What happens when commercial incentives favour a relationship that creates national-security exposure? Which information should be shared with government, and under what safeguards?

Once a private company becomes a strategic chokepoint, these are no longer purely internal corporate questions.

Nor can government simply absorb the function. NVIDIA's strategic value comes partly from the commercial ecosystem, engineering talent and global scale that state ownership would not automatically reproduce. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate private mediation, but to govern it.

The United States has treated advanced semiconductor controls primarily as a problem of denying China access to specific technologies. That approach remains important, but the emerging evidence suggests that technology denial alone is insufficient.

The chain that converts an accelerator into AI capability now includes manufacturers, server integrators, logistics firms, cloud providers, data-centre operators, software platforms, resellers, financiers and remote users. Each can become a control surface.

A chip that is legally shipped to Southeast Asia can still create a national-security problem if end use is opaque. A corporate security policy can be technically sound while senior leadership remains exposed to targeted influence. A formal export restriction can be undermined by remote access rather than physical smuggling.

The appropriate strategic unit is therefore the conversion system, not the chip.

Governance must follow the capability across the chain.

This requires more sophisticated end-use monitoring, stronger counter-intelligence cooperation with strategic firms, clearer board-level responsibility for national-security risk and better mechanisms for separating ordinary commercial relationships from relationships that create privileged access to strategic information.

It also requires caution. Governments should not use vague national-security claims to turn every foreign customer or personal relationship into presumed espionage. The danger of overreaction is real. A governance system that treats suspicion as proof would damage commercial openness, civil liberties and the credibility of legitimate counter-intelligence work.

The objective is not maximal control. It is reliable conversion governance.

The present controversy remains unresolved. The board investigation may find no compromise of NVIDIA information or US national security. Intelligence assessments reported by the press may be revised, challenged or contextualised. The evidence surrounding Megaspeed may develop in directions that are currently impossible to predict.

The analytical significance of the episode does not require those uncertainties to disappear.

NVIDIA has become sufficiently important to US technological power that allegations concerning access to its CEO triggered an independent board investigation and congressional national-security scrutiny. That reaction alone demonstrates how far the company has moved from being a successful technology firm to becoming part of the infrastructure through which state capability is produced.

The strategic lesson is therefore narrower, but more durable, than the headlines suggest.

Corporate chokepoints strengthen national AI capability only when chokepoint power is matched by national-capability integration and effective conversion governance. When those mechanisms are weak, concentration can transform strategic advantage into concentrated vulnerability.

This does not make NVIDIA less valuable to the United States. It explains why its value creates governance obligations that ordinary corporate models were not designed to carry.

The AI competition will not be decided only by who invents the best models or possesses the most advanced chips. It will also depend on whether states can govern the private nodes through which technological capacity becomes national power.

That is the deeper issue raised by the NVIDIA case, whatever the investigation ultimately finds.

This analysis applies the Geopolitics of AI capability-conversion framework: Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation, with governance operating across all three layers. The framework distinguishes possession of AI-related resources from the institutional, industrial and operational processes required to convert them into sustained strategic capability.

The NVIDIA episode is used here as a revealing case rather than as proof of espionage or compromise. The proposed idea of chokepoint inversion is a candidate mechanism for further comparative research, not an established empirical finding.

See: Anastasios (Tasos) Tassos, ‘Converting Artificial Intelligence into Strategic Power: A Three-Layer Framework for Comparative Strategy,’ Comparative Strategy (2026), DOI: 10.1080/01495933.2026.2702077.

#9702. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9701. Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

#9700. billion-context Hands-On: Compressing Coding-Agent History to Fit a Small Context Window

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

Long agent sessions keep failing the same way for me. The window fills up with test logs and file dumps, the harness runs its own auto-compaction, and the agent forgets the constraint I gave it an hour earlier. So when billion-context reached 5,427 GitHub stars about three months after the repo was created, I wanted to see what it actually does to a real session, measured in tokens and in what the agent still remembers afterwards.

This post covers what I installed, the one bug I ran into, the numbers from a real tool-calling session, and where I think the project's claims hold up and where they don't.

billion-context (github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context, MIT plus an attribution clause) is a local proxy, bili, that sits between a coding agent and its model API. It works with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google-native requests, and it adds four tools to every request:

The main difference from Claude Code-style auto-compaction is that the model decides what to fold, nudged by the proxy as the window fills. The proxy runs the fold on its side, keeps the originals in a local SQLite store, and from then on sends the folded view upstream. Summaries can be folded again (tier 2, tier 3), and the README calls this "an LSM tree over summaries."

The README makes three headline claims: "100K context is enough", "5× fewer tokens", and "month-long single sessions." The author's preprint in the repo reports 174,327 model calls over 4.5 months. A benchmark folder labeled "independent third-party" reports 79.2% vs 83.2% for full context on LongMemEval-S at 71% lower cost. Both live inside the project's own repo, so I count them as claims, not evidence.

The repo is also changing very fast: 565 commits between 2 Nov and today, and npm latest is 0.1.213. I tested that version.

I had a Free Tier Gemini key and no other credentials, so I skipped the bili claude / bili codex launchers. Instead I used the universal path: start the proxy and prefix the upstream URL with /bili/. To get folds within an afternoon's budget, I pinned the window to 40K tokens:

I set ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0 on purpose. By default bili checks npm every three minutes and upgrades itself after a staggered delay. That's convenient for a fast-moving project, but I don't want it in a benchmark, and I'd think about it before putting this on a shared CI box.

My first harness used Gemini's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The first request went through fine. Every request after a tool call failed with:

Gemini 3.x returns an opaque thought_signature with each tool call, and it has to come back in the next request. The same two-request script returned 200 when sent directly and 400 through the proxy, so the proxy is dropping that field on the chat-completions path. Switching to Gemini's native generateContent wire fixed it:

If you run Gemini 3 behind an OpenAI-style client, test multi-turn tool calls before anything else.

I wrote a small agent loop with a single bash tool and pointed it at a fresh clone of python-slugify. I scripted 11 user turns, the kind I'd actually type:

The model was gemini-3.5-flash-lite. For the baseline, I ran Gemini's countTokens on every uncompressed request prefix, using the same system prompt and tool schema without the proxy. That gives an exact "what would I have sent" number for each of the 41 requests.

One thing about the agent itself: Flash-Lite never edited a file. It read code, ran tests, and then claimed in its final answer that it had implemented the feature. The git tree was clean. That's a model problem, not a compression problem. The fold summary was actually more accurate than the model's answer, because it listed the feature under "Open objectives."

The session took 41 client requests and 184 seconds of wall-clock time. That includes three back-offs from Free Tier 429s (250K input tokens per minute); summed model latency was 45.9 seconds. The proxy added a median of 10 ms of local processing per request (max 26 ms over 50 requests).

That's 284 characters standing in for a few thousand tokens of find output, a full pytest log, and an inspect.signature dump. The user messages themselves stayed verbatim, because the proxy protects them.

I asked two quizzes at the end of the session, once through the proxy (folded view) and once directly with the full history.

Easy set (10 questions about things I told it): ticket ID, client, Python version, separator decision, new kwarg, test file, first test result, port, reviewer, postponed refactor. Through bili: 10/10 on 13,821 prompt tokens. Full history: 10/10 on 39,114. Since user turns aren't folded, this is the case the design is built for, and it held up.

Hard set (8 questions about tool output): the line number of slugify(), the module marked "DO NOT MODIFY", the CLI --algorithm choices, the last commit hash, the top CHANGELOG version, the pytest/Python versions, the parameter count, and the CLI test files.

So the folded agent matched the full-history agent, but only by paying for retrieval: six upstream rounds and 89,958 input tokens (72,497 of them cached), against one 39K call. Three practical notes. First, on the non-streaming lane the search_context output came back to my client as the response text, with no answer after it, so plan on streaming. Second, the search receipts ("Found 2 block(s) for ...") show up in the client-visible text stream, as do fold receipts. Third, in an earlier attempt the model decompressed a block to /tmp/acp-decompress-b6-*.txt and then tried to grep it with its own bash tool, so decompress-to-file assumes the agent can read local files.

At Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite list prices ($0.30/M input, $0.03/M cached, $2.50/M output):

On a 39K-token session, compression lost on cost once caching is counted. Every fold rewrites the prompt prefix, and the proxy's own log said so: "the whole prefix rewrites and the prefix cache restarts from scratch on the next request." On top of that, the ~4K-token tool overhead is charged on every call. The savings come from staying under a window you'd otherwise overflow, and from long sessions where uncompressed history grows without limit. My session was neither, so treat 12.5% as a lower bound for a short session, not as evidence for the "5×" claim.

The design idea is good: let the model decide what's stale, keep the originals, and make folds reversible. In my run that held up on the questions that matter most, the constraints and decisions I gave it, at a third of the final context size. The "billions of tokens" claim is a separate test that needs a session thousands of calls long. I'll run that one with a stronger model before I put it in front of real agent traffic.

#9699. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9698. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9697. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9696. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

Asset Protection & Asset Recovery ContextNexus.net www.linkedin.com/in/nadavgover

At the end of October, roughly $6.3 billion left Binance wallets across ten blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, about 4X times the Bybit hack of 2025, and the FBI links it to North Korea. Binance has pledged to cover all user losses.

For most readers that is where the story ends. For anyone whose assets are held by a third party, it is where the real question begins, Binance could absorb a loss of this size, could the institution that holds yours?

In less than 48 hours, about $3 billion of the stolen funds was frozen, roughly 47% of the total. More than $2.3 billion of it was frozen by Tether and Circle, the companies behind USDT and USDC. Unlike Bitcoin, these tokens are controlled by their issuers who can blacklist an address and make every token it holds impossible to spend.

Part of the loot was held in these stablecoins so the issuers were able to stop it. Binance has not said what became of the remaining $3.3 billion, and investigators warn that professional laundering networks convert crypto into cash faster than recovery teams can follow.

Recovery is a race measured in hours, and it is won by whoever reaches the parties able to stop the funds first, issuers, exchanges and courts.

Binance has two layers of protection, The first is SAFU, an emergency fund created in 2018 and held in Bitcoin, which stands at about $1 billion. The second is the company itself, Binance says it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds to cover this incident, and analysts do not see a meaningful risk to its solvency. Users are protected by the second layer, not the first.

A guarantee is only as strong as the balance sheet behind it. Very few institutions could absorb a loss six times the size of their dedicated reserve and keep operating normally, and the smaller the institution holding your assets, the less its promise is worth.

Binance chose to cover every loss, and it had the balance sheet to do it. Without such a promise you may discover only after the loss that you were never the owner of what you thought you held.

Either your assets are held separately in your name and you can take them back, or you hold a claim, and you join a line of creditors waiting for whatever is left. FTX customers spent years in that line.

On the surface you can’t tell which one you are, until trouble starts. The difference is in the fine print, and almost nobody reads it until it is too late. Capital protection starts here, asmart financial architecture decides which side of that line you stand on, and it can only be built before the loss.

The first hours decide the outcome so the preparation has to happen earlier. Ask yourself these 3 questions while everything is calm:

1. How much of my wealth is allowed to sit with any single institution?

2. Can I prove within an hour what I own and how it is held?

People who recover assets quickly are usually the ones who had already answered these questions.

Crypto vanishes in minutes. Lose a property, a company stake or an account abroad and the fight to get it back can take years.

The deciding factor is identical, what was already in place before the loss, An unbroken chain of title, an ownership structure that holds up in court and a jurisdiction chosen on purpose decide whether you recover the asset or only the right to sue for it.

Which of those 3 questions could you answer with confidence today?

Nobody Is Questioning These Structures Anymore

#9694. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9693. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9691. The AI-Native Organization: Smaller Teams, Faster Execution, Fewer Roadmaps

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

This is a time of the year where every organization is working out the structure that makes sense for them. And this year, every firm clearly has significant changes planned.

A big contributor is AI. Tools have evolved massively since the start of the year (coding tools, org harnesses, best practices), and many of us now run org structures that don’t match what’s possible today. That may be slowing us down.

But with Coding tools evolving the way they have, a lot of the “how” has collapsed.

Claude already is writing about 90% of Claude Code’s code.

Traditionally non-technical users like Marketers and Finance have also warmed up to pushing code using org provided and self owned harnesses.

As a part of this study, we have looked at a broad range of technology firms, from the large, like Amazon and Microsoft, to Shopify and Linear, as well as smaller labs like Every - and how they have evolved over the year to adapt to this new reality

A few common patterns across organizations include

Salesforce is experimenting with one-person and three-person teams. So is Meta, with three- to five-member teams. Every has redesigned the construct into “two-slice” teams: a single person running an entire product.

“We have four software products, each run by a single person.” — Dan Shipper, The Two-slice Team, Feb 13, 2026 (tweet)

Most companies have realized that the shorter the distance between idea and execution, the lower the friction. And with agents, people can have virtual team members rather than actual ones, which avoids the need for a full setup.

Companies have also started experimenting with consolidation of roles into common profiles.

For example, LinkedIn has started its builder program, where individuals in very small teams own end-to-end accountability, from customer focus to outcomes.

https://careers.linkedin.com/pathways-programs/entry-level/apb

Anthropic has stopped talking about roles, and talks more about Archetypes. They have also stopped bucketizing the roles of designers, product managers - and meld everyone into a common job title - MTS (member of technical staff), with designers pushing code, developers PM’ing and PM’s developing.

Over time, when designers and PM’s write code, engineers design and plan what to release - the functional hats everyone wears is more and more likely to transform into what each person brings to the table (growth, consumer sense, building and architecting)

When speed of decision making is key, having committees decide on the right approach is clearly a drag on time. We see firms with founder leaders taking a stronger stance.

For example, Ramp has mentioned that “everyone is a builder” and they expect nothing else from anyone in the organization.

Tobi talks about the expectation from teams on AI adoption, decisive leadership.

Harnesses are the organizational brain and actioning engine, and which practically operate through the equivalent of chat. For example, Ramp’s Inspect and Shopify’s River allows anyone in the companies to be a builder and get what they want done (Create creatives, run a campaign, develop code).

No intermediaries for capabilities that are not consumer facing.

Therefore - teams beyond engineering are coding. Whether it’s marketing or finance, all teams have started pushing code.

that owns a problem end to end for a fixed stretch. Meta is moving from teams of 10–20 to pods of 3–5. LinkedIn forms engineer, designer and PM trios for about a quarter. Roles are a lot more fluid, sure engineers write more of the code that customers see and ensure scale. But designers, PM’s and other roles also operate on code / so design as a function is not sacrosanct to designers, neither is code sacrosanct to developers. This is a slow pivot towards archetypes - from the existing role-based functions

In this new structure, The pod owner answers for the end metric itself, whether that’s revenue, retention or customer time saved, and everything else, agents included, is just how they get there.

A small platform team runs the company harness: Ramp’s 5-person Inspect team, Shopify’s River and Stripe’s Minions. The Harness acts as everyone’s virtual teammate - operatable through slack or any channel of choice. This allows for multiplayer real-time development, as well as non-engineers being able to get work done on code with limited human intervention or gatekeeping.

With teams incentivised to ship fast, that works well, until a major stability, security or compliance issue kicks in. Non-negotiable functions are gatekept (to the essential degree), and reviewed by agents (and humans) above a certain risk level. Even at Shopify, a human still reviews every production PR.

Design, growth and marketing move between pods instead of sitting inside them. They codify everything they can, and check it into the codebase for all engineers to use. But they still get involved in the most important phases of each project.

With all teams now focused significantly on outcomes and speed of delivery, it’s impossible for everybody to keep track of the latest developments in the market. That’s why there is typically also a frontier team. Its members may not be allocated full-time, but they are responsible for synthesizing what’s going on in the world and systematically bringing it into the organization. Examples are Every’s frontier team, Meta’s Agent Transformation Accelerator and Ramp’s Glass, built so the company “learns things once”.

Naturally, the next key question is how planning takes place. Are roadmaps still relevant? Are they quarterly or weekly? Are they built around goals?

Microsoft’s Copilot chief Jacob Andreou put it bluntly: “the reality is a six to twelve month roadmap doesn’t really exist.” Notion’s 2026 roadmap lists no features at all, only a principle about responding quickly to major changes. “Ditch fixed roadmap” was a callout from Slack CPO Rob Seaman.

On Claude Code, Boris Cherny sets a three-to-six-month vision and the PM works back from it. Linear keeps roughly a six-month direction but reprioritises weekly, because when building is cheap it’s easier to build the wrong thing.

Meta’s pods moved to four-week sprints instead of six-month planning cycles. HubSpot went from annual planning to six-week sprints. Tobi Lütke now calls Shopify’s own six-week review cycle “way too limiting”.

Plans are tested by shipping, not by review meetings. Most Claude Code features launch as research previews. Ramp lets teams ship to an early-access tier whenever they want, and reviews only before general release.

Clearly, every organization is different. Sometimes commercial teams and tech teams are separate. But a few things hold:

In the end, it’s clear that org structures will keep changing, and likely more often than once a year. What’s most important is for the organization to stay agile to changing needs. It’s going to be a wild ride.
