#9690. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9689. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9687. Building an AI-Powered Household Manager With Laravel and the Laravel AI SDK

Building: Auction Events Platform. Dev: Auctions, Marketplaces, NoCode, AI

Building: Auction Events Platform. Dev: Auctions, Marketplaces, NoCode, AI

Building: Auction Events Platform. Dev: Auctions, Marketplaces, NoCode, AI

Household Manager is a Laravel application I am building in public. The point is not a chat window that invents a grocery list. The point is a set of agents that already know the house, already know the pantry, and already fire at 08:00 in the user’s timezone.

The four original domains are cooking, shopping, maintenance, and cleaning. Those four are now in the app. Along the way I had to make the clock honest: a missed minute is a late run, not a skipped day.

This article is the long form of the build series I have been posting on LinkedIn and X. Same facts. Room to show how the slices lock together.

I wanted a real application for the official Laravel AI SDK, not a demo agent in Tinker. Cursor does the agentic development. The stack stays Laravel and PHP: queues, notifications, Pest, structured output, conversation memory.

Users instruct the system through a web app. Settings are plain forms. The agents do not wait for a prompt at meal time. A scheduler ticks every minute and calls them when the local clock says so.

That constraint is the whole design. If the agent only works when you open a chat, it is a recipe generator. If it works when you are not looking, it is a household manager.

Cooking was the first function that actually did something at 08:00.

Each user has a Cooking Agent. You set breakfast, lunch, and dinner times, how many people, city and country, and dietary notes as plain text. Location is geocoded so cuisine and ingredients fit the place. One of the early test households is two people, Ukrainian lunch, not too much sugar, one person diabetic.

A scheduler runs every minute. At each meal time in the user’s timezone, a job calls the agent. The agent returns structured dishes: ingredients, cooking instructions, serving instructions, and a generated photo of the plated meal. It remembers the conversation, so the menu varies instead of repeating the same dish three days in a row.

There is a Cooking settings screen and a Meals calendar. Open a day and you get breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Serving a meal is a real event. Stock goes down. Meal times do not invent extra dishes.

Planning the menu is only half of cooking. You still need to know when to start.

The Cooking Agent estimates preparation time as structured output. Each meal stores prep in minutes. Dishes run in parallel when that is practical. The same every-minute scheduler that handles serving fires at served_at - prep. Laravel Notifications sends one mail: start now, this is dinner, here are the dishes. Each meal is notified once.

A dinner served at 21:00 with about 30 minutes of prep mails at 20:30. A 00:15 meal with 30 minutes of prep notifies at 23:45 the day before. That wrap has to work or the clock is a toy.

Prep-time mail. The agent owns the clock, not only the recipe.

The second piece is a Shopping Agent on the same SDK. It reads the week’s ingredients, subtracts what is already in inventory, and that is the list. Inventory is grouped the way a store is grouped: Produce, Dairy, Meat and fish, and so on. Units follow Metric or US from Cooking settings. Each item gets a generated product photo.

The agent only puts on the list what you do not already have.

A checkbox is the wrong payload. Need 3 kg of tomatoes and the store only has 2.5? Mark 2.5. Remaining 0.5 kg stays on the list for the next stop, not a new list. Need 3 eggs and you grab 5? Stock becomes 5, and the line is done.

Each card already holds what is left to buy. One click, no typing, means you bought that amount. A different number is a short aisle or an extra pack. Inventory only rises by the amount you enter.

The trip writes a quantity. That is what I want the agent to see: bought 2.5 kg, 0.5 kg still open, stock +2.5.

A grocery list is a running remainder, not a checkbox.

Shopping time plus delivery time is counted back from Monday breakfast. A scheduled job, shopping:prepare, still runs every minute. It fires when now is at or after Monday breakfast minus that lead. A three-day lead starts next week’s list on Friday at 08:00. A nine-day lead skips a Monday that is already too close and lands on the next one that still fits.

Default is one shopping day and no delivery. You set days and hours on a Shopping times screen. Under the heading, a live line shows when the next list will start preparing.

One of the screenshots is that screen with 1 shopping day and 2 delivery days. Breakfast is 08:00 from Cooking, so the next list starts Friday, 11 September at 08:00 — three days before Monday breakfast. Groceries have to be in the house before that meal.

Once cooking and shopping were live, the safety net had to be real. Pest 5 on the Laravel AI SDK build, so a dish, a shopping list, and a pantry change cannot drift without a test noticing.

Numbers from a fresh local run at the time of that post:

Local Test Impact Analysis records which tests a change actually needs. CI still runs the full suite, including Chromium for the browser test. Coverage, evals, and mutate stay local.

Coverage that never kills a mutant is decoration. Mutation score is the number I care about.

Maintenance is not cleaning. Cleaning is mopping. Maintenance is the dryer vent, the gutters, the things that break if you forget them for a year.

A House screen records the property: floors and rooms, outbuildings (storage, BBQ cabin), inside facilities (pool, SPA, jacuzzi), outside (garden, trees, flowers), and equipment (fridge, oven, laundry, dryer, dishwasher). Save the inventory and a schedule appears. You can override cadence, season, start date, skip, or notes.

The Maintenance calendar is a month grid. Click a day for that day’s tasks. The same every-minute scheduler runs. At 08:00 in the user’s timezone, Laravel Notifications emails the day’s work. No tasks, no email.

Cooking, shopping, and maintenance all sat on that every-minute scheduler. A deploy or a crash in the due minute used to drop the task: serve the meal, mail “start cooking,” plan next week’s list, send the maintenance digest. The run was gone. Nothing tried again.

The same jobs still tick every minute. They no longer need the clock to match the due minute. If the time has passed and the work is not marked done, they run it late. A delay is fine. Skipping is not.

Same-day catch-up is bounded. Breakfast due at 08:00, scheduler back at 08:05: the meal is served. A prep mail due at 07:35 still goes. Last night’s dinner can still be served shortly after midnight. Yesterday’s breakfast is left alone.

Shopping was the extra hole. The target week used to be computed from now plus lead time, so a miss that lasted into Monday slid to the following week. Catch-up now keeps the week that was due, as long as that Monday is not more than a day in the past, and passes those dates into the job so it does not plan the wrong week.

A killed run used to hold a 24-hour overlap lock. That lock now expires in ten minutes. The queued jobs that plan meals and the shopping list retry after a worker crash, instead of failing on the first attempt.

There is no extra “did it run?” table. The meal’s serve stamp, the prep-mail stamp, the shopping-list row, and the maintenance log already record whether the work ran.

Treat a missed cron as “run it when you wake up,” not “skip this one.”

Cleaning is the fourth original domain. It is generated from the same house inventory. It is kept off the maintenance list.

Save the House screen and a cleaning schedule appears under the maintenance one. Kitchen counters daily. Vacuum and dust weekly. Bathroom weekly. Bedding weekly. Windows every three months. BBQ cabin weekly in summer. Pool skim weekly in summer. Dryer lint trap weekly — the yearly vent stays on maintenance.

You can override cadence, season, start date, skip, or notes. Skip a task and that day stays empty.

The Cleaning calendar is a month grid. Click a day for that day’s chores. At 08:00 local time, Laravel Notifications emails the work. No tasks, no email.

Cook, shop, maintain, clean. That is the original four.

The interesting part is not any one screen. It is the shared facts.

The agents produce structured output. The application records whether the work ran. I did not add a separate ledger for catch-up. The existing stamps were enough.

The public series started as a clean Laravel skeleton with the SDK already wired. The goal was to exercise the SDK in a real app:

Cursor is the development environment. The application stays in Laravel and PHP. No separate agent runtime.

What I care about next is the same thing I cared about at the start. Does the agent still do the work when nobody is looking at the screen? If the answer is yes after a deploy at 07:59, the design is holding.

Built in public on Laravel, the Laravel AI SDK, Pest, and Cursor. Short updates go to X and LinkedIn. This is the long form.

#9686. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9684. One Abuse Complaint Later: Hardening a Home Proxy Without Blocking All UDP

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

This piece continues a previous write-up on diagnosing injected TCP resets [1]. That one was about proving where a connection failed. This one is about keeping a shared exit within its provider's rules and recoverable when its own tooling fails.

The setup is boring on purpose. One cheap virtual server, a gigabit port, a proxy core (Xray) with a REALITY inbound, and a house full of devices that route through it by domain rules on the router. Nothing exotic; the build takes an evening and about twenty dollars a year. It served video, cloud sync, and late night music discovery before this incident.

Then a family member installed a torrent client.

The client did what torrent clients do. It announced itself to public trackers, joined the public DHT network through its bootstrap nodes, and started moving gigabytes at line rate. Nobody in the house noticed anything; the video streams were fine, the ping was fine, everything was fine.

Forty minutes later the hoster forwarded the first abuse complaint. The message was professionally assembled: a timestamp with a timezone, the exact protocol their sensor had matched, both endpoints of the observed flow, and a link to the acceptable use policy. The complaint documented a flow associated with the exit address. I could not reconstruct the monitoring system behind it from that notice alone.

The policy page left no room for creativity. Repeat complaints end with the address null-routed, and null-routed budget servers do not get appeal processes. The exit had to become hostile to BitTorrent, and it had to happen before the next evening, because torrent clients tend to run on schedules. Whoever starts the client, the operator of the exit answers for what leaves it.

The instinctive fix, and I almost shipped it, reads one line long: block UDP. The reasoning is sound as far as it goes. The DHT and uTP use UDP, so blocking UDP removes important paths. It does not stop TCP peer connections or every tracker.

In my incident, observed torrent traffic stopped. Several unrelated applications broke too.

The first attempt dropped every UDP flow on the exit except DNS on port 53. Torrent traffic stopped within minutes, which looked like victory for about an hour.

Messenger calls were disrupted while text messages continued to work. WhatsApp survived through TCP fallback. Blocking UDP did not make every call impossible; it made the household depend on whichever fallback each application could manage.

The split between messages and calls was the useful clue. A service could remain reachable while one of its communication paths was blocked. I removed the blanket rule and tested calls again.

QUIC was affected too. I did not measure a browser-wide latency penalty. Games and browser videoconferencing belong in the regression checklist; I did not keep controlled results for them.

That is the trap with a transport-level block: ordinary browsing and messaging can make the connection look healthy while other functions fail. A dashboard of established TCP sessions would not establish that UDP-dependent traffic still worked.

The lesson cost one evening. Blocking an entire transport was too broad for accidental BitTorrent use on this shared exit. The replacement needed narrower rules and tests of the household applications that mattered.

A client needs a way to discover peers before it can transfer data. Common starting points include trackers, DHT bootstrap nodes, and information already stored locally.

These sources overlap, but they are not a closed list. Trackers may use hostnames or IP addresses. Clients can retain peers and DHT routing tables across restarts. Torrent files may contain node addresses, and users can supply peers directly.

BEP 5 explicitly describes persistent routing tables and embedded nodes. A hostname deny list cannot remove that knowledge from a client.

The objective here is narrower: reduce the discovery paths available to ordinary household clients, while avoiding a blanket UDP block. This is a mitigation for accidental use, not a guarantee against another complaint. Where the hoster's policy requires reliable prevention, endpoint controls or keeping untrusted devices off the shared exit remain necessary.

Translated into ordered routing rules on the exit node:

Four checks are expressed as three routing rules: the protocol sniffer, tracker list, bootstrap names, and port range. The tracker list and bootstrap names share one domain rule.

These rules have two prerequisites. Enable traffic sniffing on every inbound that carries the traffic being filtered, and provide the block outbound. Merge this field into each existing inbound, keeping its listener, credentials, and transport settings:

Add this object to the existing outbounds array if the tag is not already defined:

The snippets are configuration fragments, not a replacement configuration. Keep the ordinary outbound first: it remains the default for unmatched traffic. Without enabled payload sniffing, the BitTorrent protocol rule cannot identify its handshake. bittorrent is not a destOverride value; that list controls supported hostname overrides. Here, routeOnly: true uses the sniffed hostname for routing without replacing the connection's destination address. If the inbound already has a sniffing policy, reconcile it rather than replacing it blindly.

The protocol sniffer catches plain BitTorrent handshakes on any port. Honesty matters here, and the documentation is refreshingly blunt about it: the built-in sniffer is basic and may miss encrypted or obfuscated handshakes. Treat it as a tripwire, not a wall. Its usefulness depends on the handshake that actually reaches the sniffer.

The tracker list is a community-maintained geosite category. Its coverage changes, so verify the domains relevant to your clients instead of assuming it includes every default tracker.

The four DHT names in the rule above are useful bootstrap targets to cover, not a universal or mandatory bootstrap set. Other names, direct addresses, saved routing tables, and embedded nodes can bypass them.

A domain rule needs a domain to match. DNS resolution on a laptop does not automatically reveal that name to the exit server. What matters is what the proxy receives or can recover.

A proxy destination containing a hostname

Confirm the client actually sends the hostname

An IP destination with a supported name-bearing handshake

Inspect the configured sniffer and routing behavior

The packet need not contain the bootstrap name

A cached peer or manually entered address

That distinction explains a frustrating test result: the list can contain the right hostname while the connection still passes. Adding more names will not fix missing name visibility.

The installer below is idempotent. It cleans its tagged rules before writing replacements, including the blanket-UDP attempt from Part 2. Re-running it does not duplicate its tagged rules. The marker uses Xray's documented ruleTag field. Review the two legacy shapes before using it: exact equality cannot prove who originally created a rule. The installer assumes the inbound sniffing settings and block outbound are already configured.

Run the installer with permission to preserve the original file's owner and group. My service reads a root:xray configuration with mode 0640. Copying only that mode to a root-created temporary file can leave it owned by root:root, making the replacement unreadable to the service. The snippet preserves ownership before replacement and creates the temporary file privately. A successful validation as root does not prove that the service account can read it; check the configuration under the actual service user before restarting.

Testing covered three properties, because duplicates are not the only way to fail. A double run produced no duplicated rules, because cleanup now keys on the ruleTag and cannot miss its own output. A scratch config carrying a foreign UDP rule and a foreign bittorrent-shaped rule kept both untouched: only tagged rules and the two known pre-tag shapes are removed. The write path goes through a backup, a temporary file, an Xray configuration test, and an atomic replace. The code writes the file; applying it to the running service is a separate step. An earlier version matched every UDP rule as removable, and the one after it read one field while writing another, creating a duplicate per run. Both mistakes stay in this paragraph as a warning: installers are code, and code needs tests.

One more bug survived the test doubles. Xray infers the configuration format from the filename unless told otherwise; config.json.tmp has an unsupported extension. My stub returned success without checking that. On Xray 26.3.27 for macOS arm64, the old installer failed with "Failed to get format" and left the original file untouched. The correction explicitly selects JSON. The final snippet, including mkstemp and ownership preservation, then passed two runs as root with real Xray 26.3.27 for Linux arm64 in a disposable container. Both runs preserved foreign rules and root:xray ownership with mode 0640; validation also passed as the xray user. An invalid configuration was rejected without replacing the original or leaving a temporary file. These checks exercise configuration loading and file access, not live traffic filtering.

Choose a tracker URL that answers through the unfiltered route. Use its real protocol; an HTTPS request to a UDP-only tracker is not a useful control.

A timeout or TLS failure alone does not identify the blocking component. Compare the same endpoint with the relevant rule disabled, then enabled, and correlate the result with routing logs. Run a reachable control request too. Do this in a controlled test window, using authorized content and a test device.

The following matrix makes the boundary visible before trusting the policy:

Fresh client, selected tracker and bootstrap paths

A rule match and failed discovery on those paths

Same client with retained peers or DHT state

Whether transfers resume despite hostname filters

Call or QUIC session through the same exit

Every application or UDP port is unaffected

Hostname filtering can see raw IP traffic

Record the Xray version, client version, rule order, and whether the client state was fresh. A screenshot of an idle torrent client omits all four.

Do not pipe curl into head and treat the pipeline status as curl's result. Without pipefail, a successful final command can hide an earlier failure. Capture the status of the command being tested directly.

Four other designs got considered and rejected before the layered approach, and the reasons are instructive.

Blocking torrents on the router by DNS failed for two reasons. First, devices with hardcoded DNS or DNS-over-HTTPS bypass the router resolver entirely, and the exit cannot assume every device uses its resolver. Second, DNS filtering says nothing about direct IP connections, and DHT speaks raw UDP to addresses.

Per-device policing, the management answer, does not survive contact with guests and phones. It also pushes the problem onto people who cannot debug it, which converts an engineering task into a series of arguments.

Port-based blocking alone, without the domain layers, fails because modern clients randomize their listening ports on first run. The 6881-6889 range stays in the rule set anyway, as a cheap belt under the suspenders, but nothing depends on it.

Rate limiting torrent-shaped traffic was the most tempting sophisticated option and the easiest to reject. Shaping requires classifying the flow, which returns to the encrypted-handshake problem, and slower traffic can still participate in a monitored swarm. Lower transfer speed does not eliminate the risk of an abuse complaint.

Some client networks, mostly mobile, drop long-lived connections. On those paths the TCP profile sometimes failed in a recognizable pattern: a TLS handshake error, then timeouts, while ICMP still answered. A second inbound using the XHTTP transport in stream-one mode, on the same routing table, worked where the TCP profile failed in my tests. I did not determine why the paths behaved differently; the second inbound is a comparison path, not a diagnosis.

The full transport story, including the sniffing trap that silently disables domain rules when clients resolve locally, belongs in its own write-up. Two details travel with this article because they cost an hour each: in this tested configuration, Vision belongs on the TCP profile; the XHTTP profile omits that flow flag. Sniffing can recover supported names when a client sends an IP destination. Connections already addressed by hostname do not need sniffing for that name to be available.

A later experiment with an additional TLS endpoint exposed another test boundary. Server-side checks passed: the publicly trusted certificate validated, and the listener accepted requests. From the household client, traffic still stalled; an independent client reproduced the failure. The same request sent through an SSH forward to the same listener completed. That comparison placed the failure on the direct network path rather than in the server configuration, without identifying its cause. I removed the experimental endpoint. A server-side smoke test had never proved that the household could use it.

A defense built on domain lists is only as fresh as the lists, so the exit needs a geo database update job. This section exists because mine failed in the most educational way possible.

An installer download returned HTML instead of shell source. My preserved setup guide used the form bash -c "$(curl ...)": command substitution puts the response into a single command-line argument. A large response can exceed the operating system's argument limit before Bash parses any of it. That is consistent with the recorded "Argument list too long" failure. Piping a response into Bash's standard input is a different mechanism; it does not hit that argument-size limit.

The recovery lesson was to stop treating a downloaded response as executable source before checking it. The smaller updater below fetches only data files, validates the configuration that uses them, and attempts to restore the old files if replacement fails.

The following Linux example updates databases only. It does not update the Xray binary or systemd unit. It assumes both old database files exist and runs with permission to replace them and restart Xray. It requires flock, supplied by util-linux on Ubuntu.

The lock is acquired before downloads, backups, or replacements. A competing invocation exits without touching the shared backup files. Every updater that writes these databases must use the same lock path. The shell keeps file descriptor 9 open through recovery and releases the lock on exit; keep the lock file in place rather than deleting it. A different updater that ignores this lock can still race with the example.

In the Linux container test, a held lock rejected a competing invocation before any download, backup, or service command. With the lock free, the updater completed and released it on exit. The test used real flock and Xray validation; downloads and service-control commands were test doubles.

An active process is the first health check, not the last. Confirm every expected listener with ss -lntp, using the ports in your configuration. Then send a control request through the actual client profile. A local request on the VPS bypasses the inbound and cannot substitute for that test. These checks remain separate from the small database-update script.

The -f flag makes curl fail on HTTP errors, explicit failure branches cover the mutation steps; set -e provides additional exit behavior with shell-specific exceptions, the size floors catch truncation, and the first-byte check rejects a leading <. It misses HTML with leading whitespace and many other invalid payloads. None of that proves the database is valid, so the pipeline ends by asking Xray itself: config validation, restart, health check, and a rollback to the saved copies if any step objects. The updater attempts to restore the previous databases and restart Xray. Both restore copies are attempted, and backups are retained. An incomplete restore stops before restart and reports that manual intervention is required. Claiming more than that would be selling the guards past what they do.

The meta-lesson generalizes past geo databases: an update pipeline is a threat surface against your own infrastructure, and it deserves the same paranoia as a public endpoint.

The original failure taught me to test the updater's recovery path separately from a normal update. Replacing curl, systemctl, and the installer with test doubles lets a local harness force failures without changing a server.

There are three separate questions. Did the script exit with failure? Did it restore the previous files? Can the service start with those files? A passing answer to the first says nothing about the other two.

For the database-only example, inject a failure into each install, configuration validation, restart, and the active-state check. Compare restored file contents with the saved originals. Also fail each restore copy independently. Verify that both copies are attempted and the backups remain. Fail recovery validation and restart separately; each must report failure without claiming recovery.

A full binary updater needs more tests. Preserve executable permissions, unit files, and the previous presence or absence of installer-created paths. A backup command returning success is not enough; verify that the expected backup exists and contains the original data.

These are suggested release checks, not claims that a stubbed service models a live kernel. A local harness can prove script branches and file restoration. It cannot prove that an upstream archive, service manager, or network behaves exactly like the stub.

Test the snippets extracted from the article itself. A passing test of a different working copy does not verify what the reader will run.

Correct routing rules were not the end of hardening this exit. A later slowdown exposed a different limit: Linux was under TCP memory pressure while hundreds of megabytes of system RAM remained available.

Selected destinations then used a separate process: Xray forwarded them to warp-svc through a loopback SOCKS listener. An October 27 audit of WARP 2026.8.2115.0 found 33 socket descriptors in TCP_CLOSE holding 115.26 MiB, plus six sockets in FIN_WAIT2 holding another 28.59 MiB. Global TCP memory was 144.72 MiB. Two snapshots thirty seconds apart showed the same allocations; some half-closed connections had retained data for over forty minutes.

TCP_CLOSE described the protocol state. The process still held descriptors referring to those sockets, and their buffers remained charged. The initial ss output did not account for all of it. Following the process's descriptors, duplicating them with pidfd_getfd, and querying SO_MEMINFO and TCP_INFO found the missing allocations. The audit did not read payloads or close the original descriptors.

Restarting only WARP, without changing Xray or its configuration, reduced global TCP memory from 144.72 to 6.11 MiB. A new half-closed WARP socket soon retained about 5 MiB again. The restart identified the process holding the buffers; it did not establish the internal defect or eliminate its cause. Nor was tcp_fin_timeout a general cleanup switch: the Linux documentation defines it for orphaned FIN_WAIT_2 connections, whereas this socket still had an application reference.

A bounded reproduction bypassed Xray and used WARP's SOCKS listener directly. It mixed completed uploads, cancelled downloads, and uploads whose destination replied before consuming the body. Early-response cases retained buffers thirty seconds after completion in two of three runs. The third retained none at that checkpoint. All three actually used H3, even when warp-cli displayed an H2 setting. Requesting a transport had not proved it was in use.

An isolated replacement test used Xray 26.10.21's native MASQUE outbound with verified H2. After six rounds totaling thirty requests, the test instance's cgroup memory fell to 9.93 MiB two minutes after the workload ended. Implementation and device registration changed too, so this was not a controlled H2-versus-H3 comparison.

After migration, the old loopback hop was gone. Absence of its sockets could not prove that the replacement released its own buffers: native MASQUE uses a userspace network stack. Roughly forty-six hours later, the production Xray instance's cgroup held 25.08 MiB, including 23.45 MiB of anonymous memory, with a peak of 187.01 MiB of unknown timing and cause. That cgroup peak and the old kernel socket allocation measure different things. Four additional TCP-pressure episodes totaled about 6.6 seconds; their cause was also unknown. The snapshot showed memory had fallen, not permanent leak elimination.

A successful response establishes delivery. Hardening also means checking what remains allocated after completion, cancellation, and an early response. Otherwise, a correct traffic policy can still leave the next evening's allowed traffic competing for resources held by finished requests.

Scope: this article covers running a personal proxy within a hosting provider's acceptable use policy. Check your provider's terms and the laws that apply where you and your users are before operating one.

#9683. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9682. 15 free AI tools that are legitimately useful in 2026 (no credit card needed)

No demos, no three-day trials, and no "free" plans that only unlock features you'd never touch. These are permanently free tiers with their real limits spelled out, verified in June 2026.

Most "free AI tools" lists are built to earn affiliate commissions, not to save you time. The top-ranked tool is usually the one that pays best. The free limits get described in the haziest terms possible. And the credit card requirement hides three clicks deep in the signup flow.

This list follows different rules. Every tool here can be started without entering payment details. Limits are stated exactly, whether that's queries, images, or minutes per month. And for each tool, I point to the spot where the paywall begins, so you know before you build a workflow around something that will eventually cut you off.

I verified all 15 in June 2026. Free-tier limits change often, so check each current pricing page before you make any decision based on what's written here.

Free tier: Access to Claude Sonnet 4.6 with a daily message limit. No credit card required, and you can sign up with just an email.

Claude is the strongest free choice for serious writing: long-form analysis, document review, editing passes on your own drafts, and any job where nuance and careful reasoning count for more than speed. Its free-tier context window also copes with long documents that other free tools find difficult.

The limit to know about is the daily message cap, which heavy users will notice. The workable strategy is to spend your Claude messages on the day's most important tasks, and let a less capable free tool handle quick questions. Once the limit resets, Claude is available again.

Free tier: Unlimited standard searches and 5 Pro searches per day. No credit card required.

Perplexity does one thing better than any other free tool: cited research. Every answer links back to its source, so any claim can be checked in under a minute. If you fact-check your own content before publishing, this workflow is noticeably faster than running Google searches and reading through links one by one.

Five Pro searches a day disappear fast during serious research, and a researcher could use all five before lunch. Save them for your most complex, multi-source questions. Standard searches have no daily cap and can handle everything else.

Free tier: Full R1 model access with no daily message limit. No credit card required.

DeepSeek offers the most generous free tier among AI assistants. The R1 model holds its own against premium alternatives on reasoning, coding, and structured analysis, and the chat interface costs nothing. If you want a capable AI with no usage ceiling, DeepSeek is the practical answer right now.

4. Google NotebookLM (notebooklm.google.com)

Free tier: 100 notebooks, 50 sources per notebook, and up to 500,000 words per source. Requires a Google account but no credit card.

NotebookLM tackles hallucination by design: it answers only from the documents you upload. Give it a research paper, a company report, a product manual, or a stack of your own notes, then ask questions about those specific files. If the answer isn't in your sources, it says so instead of inventing one. That restriction sounds limiting, yet it's exactly what makes the tool useful for serious research.

Audio Overviews, which turn your uploaded documents into a podcast-style conversation, is the most surprising free capability I found anywhere on this list. Upload a dense technical report, generate an audio overview, and listen to it on your commute. For most people the free limits are effectively unlimited, since very few maintain more than 100 notebooks.

5. Elicit (elicit.com) Free tier: Unlimited searches across 200 million-plus research papers. No credit card required.

Elicit is a research assistant built specifically for scientific literature. Ask something like "what does the research show about intermittent fasting and cognitive performance?" and it searches the academic literature, pulls out key findings from the most relevant papers, and flags where the evidence contradicts itself. For anyone who reads academic papers regularly, that saves hours on each literature review compared with keyword searching in Google Scholar.

Deeper extraction, such as pulling specific data columns from several papers at once, needs a paid plan. For finding out which papers exist and what they found, the free tier is complete.

6. Grammarly (grammarly.com) Free tier: Grammar and spelling correction across your browser. No credit card required.

The free tier of Grammarly earns its place through reach. It works in Gmail, Google Docs, LinkedIn, Slack, Twitter, and most other text fields in Chrome without any manual step: you write, and it checks. That passive integration is why it's worth keeping installed even if you only ever use the free features.

Clarity rewrites, tone adjustments, and the 2026 strategic rewrite features require Premium at $12/month. People who write plain English about everyday topics will find the free grammar and spelling layer sufficient. The upgrade starts to pay off if you write often in professional settings where tone calibration matters.

7. Microsoft Copilot (copilot.microsoft.com)

Free tier: GPT-class model access with web search, plus unlimited DALL-E 3 image generation. Requires a Microsoft account but no credit card.

Microsoft Copilot is worth installing mainly for its image generation. Unlimited DALL-E 3 images through Bing Image Creator, with no subscription, make this the least-discussed free tier in AI. DALL-E 3 handles photorealism, stylized art, and marketing graphics at a quality that costs $20/month on other platforms.

As a chat tool, Copilot runs a GPT-class model with built-in web search, which suits current-events research. Its conversations are somewhat shallower than Claude's or Perplexity's on complex analytical work. For quick research queries paired with high-quality image generation, though, this free combination is hard to beat.

8. GitHub Copilot Free (github.com/features/copilot)

Free tier: 2,000 code completions and 50 chat messages per month, integrated into VS Code. Requires a GitHub account but no credit card.

GitHub Copilot Free launched in December 2024 and remains one of the more meaningful free tiers in developer tooling. Completion runs right inside VS Code or JetBrains IDEs, suggesting the next line or block as you type, with no trip to a browser tab. The integration is the feature: having AI assistance in the editor rather than in a separate chat window changes how you use it day to day.

2,000 completions a month sounds generous until you see how fast an active coding session can burn through them. It's plenty for part-time developers, or for engineers who call on Copilot only in unfamiliar territory. Those who write code every day will hit the ceiling regularly and face the $10/month upgrade question.

Free tier: 2,000 completions and 50 slow AI requests per month. No credit card required.

Cursor is an AI-first code editor built on VS Code, and it weaves Claude and GPT-class models into the editing experience more deeply than Copilot does. The free Hobby tier includes code generation, multi-file context awareness, and the ability to ask chat questions about your whole codebase. For developers deciding whether AI-assisted editing suits their workflow, it offers enough to find out before committing to $20/month.

The "slow requests" label on free-tier queries has real consequences. Responses come from lower-priority server capacity, so waits range from slightly longer to genuinely frustrating at peak hours. If latency bothers you, use the free tier off-peak.

Free tier: 10 credits per week, about 40 images. No credit card required.

Ideogram cracked the problem that kept AI image generation professionally useless for years: text inside images. Most models produced garbled, unreadable lettering even with clear typographic instructions. Ideogram 3.0 reliably renders legible headlines, poster copy, and social card text. For creators making thumbnails, marketing graphics, and social visuals that contain words, it's the free tool that actually delivers.

Ten credits a week covers a weekly content workflow if you're deliberate about what you generate. Each credit set produces four image variations from one prompt, so 10 credits means 40 images, enough for most personal or small-business needs.

Free tier: 25 generative credits per month. Requires an Adobe account but no credit card.

Adobe Firefly makes the list for one reason other image tools can't match: commercial IP indemnification. Adobe trained Firefly only on licensed content, so its images have a much cleaner copyright status than output from tools trained on scraped web material. For businesses using AI images in commercial work, that difference carries real legal weight. Twenty-five credits a month is limited, but you can spend them without a legal question mark hanging over the result.

Free tier: 10,000 characters per month, roughly 10 minutes of audio. No credit card required.

ElevenLabs became the quality benchmark for AI voice generation because its output sounds like a recording rather than synthesis. The prosody, pacing, and emotional inflection are consistently more natural than competing tools. Ten thousand characters a month works out to about 10 minutes of finished audio, enough for podcast intros, short voiceovers, product demo narration, or one explainer video per month.

On commercial licensing: under ElevenLabs' current terms, free-tier audio generally can't be used commercially. Check the latest terms before putting free-tier audio into any revenue-generating project. The paid tier starts at $5/month and explicitly includes commercial rights.

Free tier: 50 credits per day, about 10 songs. No credit card required.

Suno turns a text prompt into a full song with lyrics, instrumentation, and vocals. Describe a genre, mood, theme, and tempo, and it delivers a complete track in under a minute. Quality improved considerably in 2026, and the results are now genuinely usable as background music, content backdrops, or creative projects.

The same commercial restriction applies: under Suno's terms, free-tier songs can't be used commercially. For personal use, creative exploration, or testing whether AI music fits a future paid workflow, the free tier is remarkably generous. Ten songs a day from a text prompt is a lot of creative capacity for zero dollars.

Free tier: AI video editing, auto-captions, background removal, and a template library. No credit card required.

The free tier of CapCut packs in more AI video editing than competing tools lock behind paywalls. Auto-captioning transcribes video and places subtitles accurately in multiple languages, with no manual timing. Background removal works on video, not just on images. And the template library covers short-form formats for Reels, TikTok, and Shorts without manual editing.

Some of CapCut's AI features run on a credit system that depletes with heavier generation tasks. Editing tools and auto-captions are free and unlimited, while generative features such as AI avatars and scene generation draw from a credit pool. Work out which category your planned use falls into before relying on the free tier at scale.

Free tier: 400 AI credits, about 10 full presentations. No credit card required.

Gamma generates presentations, documents, and single-page websites from a text prompt. Its output quality sits well above other AI presentation tools: layouts look designed rather than generated, and the visual hierarchy makes sense on the first pass. Describe the content and structure you want, and Gamma returns a complete slide deck with images, text, and consistent formatting.

Ten presentations on the free tier is enough to evaluate the tool, complete a project, and decide whether the $10/month Plus plan suits you. Free exports carry a "Made with Gamma" watermark that only paid access removes. For internal decks or personal use, it's a minor annoyance. For client-facing work, factor it in.

How to stack these into a complete workflow

These free tiers work better together than alone. A practical free stack covers four areas without overlap:

Primary AI assistant: Claude for quality-sensitive writing, and DeepSeek for high-volume tasks once Claude's daily limit runs out. Research: Perplexity for cited, current-web research, and NotebookLM for analyzing documents you already have. Images: Microsoft Copilot for unlimited photorealistic or stylized images, Ideogram for images with readable text, and Adobe Firefly for anything commercially sensitive. Audio and content: ElevenLabs for voice, Suno for music, CapCut for video editing, and Gamma for presentations. Together, this stack covers what a $60-100/month AI subscription bundle might offer, for free. The honest constraint is time, not money: learning the quirks of 15 tools takes longer than learning one paid platform in depth. Start with the two or three that match your biggest bottlenecks, and add others as needs arise.

The gap between free and paid AI in 2026 is real, but it's narrower than vendors would like you to believe. The free tier of most serious AI platforms now delivers 70-80% of the paid value for the average user. The remaining 20-30% behind the paywall is the part that matters most for heavy professional use.

Free-tier limits change. Companies add payment requirements, lower message caps, or retire free tiers entirely when funding pressure or valuation targets bite. A tool that's free today is more likely to turn paid in 2027 than it was in 2022. The safest way to use any free AI tool is to build workflows without a single point of failure, so that if one tool's free tier tightens, you already have a fallback.

The best free AI tools of 2026 are free by design, not free by promotion. That distinction matters for anything you plan to use for longer than three months. The 15 tools above got their free tiers through one of three routes: open-source models, freemium business models with clear paid upsells, or platform strategies in which free usage builds ecosystem lock-in. Each route can produce stable free access over time, and each has seen free tiers walked back at some point. Confirm the current status before committing your workflow to any of them.

Everything on this list works today, for free, with no credit card. Start with the tool that addresses your biggest current time drain, and build from there.
