Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9659. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

#9657. Seedream 5.5 vs 5.0 Pro: check the output contract before migrating

Seedream 5.5 is worth evaluating for repeated image edits, transparent assets, and dense Chinese or English text. It is not an automatic replacement for a 5.0 Pro integration that depends on separate layers or exact dimensions.

The engineering question is whether improved model behavior arrives through an API that still delivers the outputs your application requires. Keep those two checks separate.

ByteDance's November 9, 2026 announcement describes 100 successive edits to one person. Each round uses the previous output as its reference, rather than returning to the original. That distinction matters when evaluating accumulated drift.

ByteDance claims pixel-level preservation of unedited regions, less color shift and detail loss, and more realistic lighting, skin, and materials. These are vendor claims and a vendor demonstration—not an independently established durability limit. The sequence does not guarantee unchanged identity, geometry, or lettering across every production job.

For dense Chinese and English text, including small lettering, the vendor reports 0.4% severe corruption and 1.7% minor corruption in its evaluation. These are not universal error probabilities. Labels, prices, and layouts still need proofreading.

The official image-generation API documentation provides this baseline:

The 5.0 Pro entries describe the official vendor API. Its layer decomposition produces a base image and independently editable PNG layers. Layer decomposition also supports the default size value auto, subject to documented dimension bounds. Better image quality does not replace that output structure.

Transparency needs a separate distinction. The official API already supports transparent editing for 5.0 Pro and Flash, with exactly one alpha-bearing input image and PNG output. The 5.5 launch instead describes native RGBA generation from text or reference images, including full and partial transparency. It is not accurate to say that 5.0 could not handle transparency.

A PNG can be fully opaque. The model-level RGBA announcement does not establish a working gateway parameter, and choosing PNG alone does not confirm transparent output.

AIHubMix's model guide documents model ID doubao-seedream-5-5 and POST /ai/v1/images/generations. The gateway image-generation guide explains the protocol.

As of November 12, 2026, 06:05 UTC, the model-specific endpoint schema:

These are published schema entries, not verified 5.5 runtime support. They establish neither successful requests nor failures. Treat this as an unresolved documentation/runtime boundary, especially if dimensions or alpha output are mandatory.

The official Volcano Ark price table documents 5.0 Pro's CNY rates but lists neither 5.5 nor the announced 5.5 Pro. The documented rates and remaining gaps are:

The 5.0 Pro prices cover ordinary generation, not layer decomposition. The first reference image is free; each additional reference costs CNY 0.02. A 2048 × 2048 output contains 4,194,304 pixels, placing it in the CNY 0.60 tier, not CNY 0.30.

Sina Technology's launch report describes 5.5 billing for input and output images, with text tokens uncharged. It gives approximately CNY 0.28 for a 2K-square edit. This is a press-reported example, not a verified complete official tariff or an AIHubMix quote.

Three such rounds would be 3 × CNY 0.28 ≈ CNY 0.84, assuming an existing source image, one reference and one output per round, no extra candidates or retries, and an unchanged rate. This is arithmetic, not a measured bill. Do not derive a precise savings percentage from a rounded report and a different model's official schedule.

ByteDance has announced a future 5.5 Pro, but the cited material establishes neither its release date nor its price. The current 5.5 is not that future Pro edition.

Start with what the output must preserve, then decide whether the model and serving route meet that requirement together.

#9654. ZIG Finance Opens $100M Vault to Bring Saudi Arabia's SME Lending Boom Onchain

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Private credit, the business of lending to companies outside the public bond market and the banking system, has grown into a market of more than $2 trillion that Moody's expects to approach $4 trillion by 2030. A growing slice of it now lives onchain. Private credit makes up about 44% of the $51 billion market for tokenized real-world assets, which puts roughly $22 billion of loans on public blockchains, while onchain private credit grew about 180% in a year to early 2026.

Saudi Arabia is one of the fastest-growing credit markets feeding that demand. Lending to Saudi small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) reached SR468 billion, or about $124.6 billion, at the end of 2025, up 33% in a year, while Vision 2030 aims to lift SMEs' share of total credit from 11.5% to 20%. Global institutions have had few direct routes into those loans, since most are made by local banks and lending platforms.

ZIG Finance launched the zEMS Vault on 11 November 2026 to open that route. The vault gives eligible institutional investors exposure to a diversified pool of Saudi SME private credit on BNB Chain, with subscriptions and redemptions in stablecoins. It is the first product from ZIG Finance's strategic partnership with Laser Digital, the digital assets subsidiary of Japanese bank Nomura, which acts as risk framework advisor, while the zEMS onchain strategy targets a raise of $100 million.

Private credit has been one of the fastest-growing asset classes since the 2008 financial crisis, as banks pulled back from riskier lending and specialist funds stepped in. Moody's puts global assets under management at more than $2 trillion, with a forecast of close to $4 trillion by 2030, as insurers, pension funds and wealthy investors look for income above public bond yields.

Tokenization, the process of recording ownership of an asset as a digital token on a blockchain, is bringing that market to new investors. Private credit overtook US Treasury products in 2026 to become the largest category of tokenized real-world assets, at about 44% of the market against 30% for Treasuries, with the total market up 42% so far in 2026. Onchain private credit products have typically offered yields of about 8% to 12%, compared with 4% to 5% for tokenized Treasuries, which explains the appetite.

Saudi lending to SMEs has grown at one of the fastest rates of any major credit market. Credit to micro, small and medium enterprises rose from SR307.4 billion in the second quarter of 2024 to SR351.7 billion by the end of that year, then to SR420.7 billion by mid-2025 and SR468 billion by the end of 2025. That is a 52% rise in 18 months (our arithmetic), while SMEs' share of total credit climbed from about 9.6% to 11.5%.

The growth is driven by Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's economic plan, which aims to lift the SME share of credit to 20% and SMEs' contribution to GDP to 35%. Banks provide about 95% of SME credit today, with financing companies providing the rest, which leaves wide room for non-bank lenders and outside investors as the target approaches. Reaching 20% from 11.5% means SME credit has to keep growing faster than total lending for years.

Private credit is becoming a major source of growth capital across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the six-country bloc that includes Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Private debt deployed in the region grew from about $0.5 billion in 2024 to $4.1 billion in 2025, overtaking venture capital at $3.3 billion, while Saudi Arabia accounted for about $3.9 billion of the total.

The demand is far larger than the supply. GCC SMEs face a credit gap of more than $250 billion, with SMEs receiving less than 10% of bank lending across the region, while global managers including King Street have announced plans to deploy billions in Saudi private credit. Industry estimates expect Gulf private credit to grow 15% to 30% a year over the next five years, as Fortune has noted in its coverage of the region.

The vault is issued by a segregated portfolio of ZM Structured Products SPC Limited, a company in the British Virgin Islands whose segregated portfolios keep each product's assets and liabilities separate. Merritt Administrators, which trades as ZIG Finance and is an authorized financial services provider regulated by South Africa's Financial Sector Conduct Authority, acts as curator. Investors hold vault tokens and do not own the underlying loans directly.

Each partner covers one part of the chain. Beehive originates the loans, Zamanat structures the product and provides Sharia advisory so it can meet Islamic finance principles, Laser Digital supports the design of the risk governance framework and gives tokenization advice, while ZIG Markets handles issuance, curation and distribution on BNB Chain. KAIO, the tokenization platform built by Laser Digital and WebN, runs tokenization, compliance and lifecycle management, including know-your-customer (KYC) checks at subscription and redemption.

The structure is also expected to include Khalij as the Sharia certification partner, with an independent calculation agent to be appointed separately. A Sharia-aligned structure opens the vault to investors who follow Islamic finance rules, a pool that the Islamic Financial Services Board puts at about $4.4 trillion of industry assets in 2025.

Beehive brings the lending base. Founded in Dubai in 2014, it was the first peer-to-peer lending platform in the Middle East and North Africa to be regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. It has funded more than $1 billion for more than 2,100 SMEs across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman. Its Saudi entity is subject to regulatory approval, while its UAE and Oman businesses are regulated by the DFSA and Oman's FSA.

KAIO brings the onchain rails. The platform has transacted more than $500 million in volume across more than 10 blockchains, with institutional funds from partners including BlackRock, Brevan Howard, Hamilton Lane, Laser Digital and Mubadala Capital live on it. Laser Digital, which Nomura set up to bridge traditional and crypto markets, is regulated by Dubai's VARA and ADGM's FSRA and registered with Japan's FSA.

ZIG Finance ties the pieces together. Its ecosystem includes ZIGChain, a layer 1 blockchain built for institutional finance, ZIG Markets as its distribution layer and the ZIG token. Laser Digital became a strategic investor and risk partner in ZIGChain in August 2026, with the two companies setting a target of at least $100 million in total value locked across several onchain credit products.

The vault launches on BNB Chain, one of the most active networks for tokenized assets. Real-world assets on the chain grew from about $3 billion in March 2026 to $5.2 billion in July, a 73% rise in four months (our arithmetic), making it the second-largest RWA network behind Ethereum with a 14.9% share.

The vault's design is about managing credit risk in the open. ZIG Finance's stated aim is to make the risk of lending to Saudi SMEs transparent and manageable, so institutional investors can get comfortable with an asset class they could not otherwise access at scale. Laser Digital's role is to help design ZIG Finance's own risk framework and the tokenization and issuance structure, with responsibility for credit selection and risk management resting with ZIG Finance and the originator.

The product carries the risks of any private credit investment. The vault does not guarantee returns, is not principal-protected and is not a deposit, while credit risk remains tied to the underlying SME borrowers. Laser Digital and Nomura do not guarantee, underwrite or rate the loans. The product is available only to eligible institutional investors in selected jurisdictions, excluding US persons and residents of Canada and Australia.

The zEMS Vault is the first product milestone in ZIG Finance's partnership with Laser Digital, which targets a minimum of $100 million in total value locked across multiple product rollouts. The companies describe the vault's architecture as a template that can be applied to other emerging markets and credit strategies, combining local origination with institutional risk governance, compliant tokenization and broader distribution.

Further opportunities across the region and other asset classes are already under consideration. A $100 million raise would equal about 10% of the more than $1 billion Beehive has funded since 2014 and about 0.08% of Saudi SME credit outstanding (our arithmetic), which shows how much room the model has to grow if it works.

Saudi SME credit is growing by tens of billions of riyals a year, Gulf private debt grew eightfold in 2025 and tokenized private credit has become the largest category of onchain real-world assets. The zEMS Vault sits where those three trends meet, giving global institutions a regulated, Sharia-aligned and stablecoin-settled route into a market that has mostly been funded by local banks.

The first test is the $100 million raise and how the loan pool performs through its first cycles. If the structure gains traction, ZIG Finance and Laser Digital plan to apply the same model to more GCC and emerging-market credit, turning a single vault into a pipeline that connects local lenders with global onchain capital.

This article is for information only and does not constitute investment advice or an offer of any product. The zEMS Vault is available only to eligible institutional investors in eligible jurisdictions, does not guarantee returns and carries the risk of loss of the entire investment.

#9653. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9651. FreeBSD Surveys 140 Developers on AI: 16% Favor a Ban, 91% Prioritize Human Accountability

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at joho-todai.com • AI-assisted

FreeBSD's Q3 2026 report includes an AI survey of 140 developers. Just 16% favor rejecting AI-assisted code outright. Meanwhile, AI scrapers keep attacking the project's infrastructure as developers work out the terms for accepting AI.

FreeBSD Core Team members surveyed project developers about their use of AI and large language models (LLMs). 140 people responded.

The results show broad support for setting terms for AI use. 88% wanted some form of project AI policy. Of all respondents, 49% wanted a formal written policy and 39% thought lightweight guidelines would suffice. Only 6% wanted the project to explicitly discourage AI, and 3% said existing contribution rules were enough.

Responses split four ways on how to handle code produced with AI assistance. The largest share, 35%, wanted mandatory disclosure. Another 25% wanted stricter review than for human-written code, and 22% favored treating it like any other contribution. The smallest group, 16%, wanted it rejected outright.

In July 2026, GCC formally adopted a policy (in Japanese) rejecting LLM-generated code longer than roughly 15 lines. In Void Linux, a maintainer dropped 113 packages at once after being accused of violating its AI policy (in Japanese). QEMU moved from a blanket ban to allowing limited use under certain conditions (in Japanese). As projects take different approaches, FreeBSD's survey shows what its developers themselves think.

The breakdown shows that developers want conditions for using AI, with outright rejection attracting less support.

The most popular safeguard was mandatory human review, at 78%. Mandatory disclosure followed at 69%, documentation of provenance and licensing at 47%, and mandatory testing at 39%. Some 48% wanted AI use always disclosed and 36% wanted disclosure only for substantial involvement, giving 84% in favor of some disclosure. Marking AI use in commit logs drew 79% support, and naming the tool drew 56%.

Asked which principles the project should prioritize, 91% chose human accountability, the top response. Transparency drew 78%. Maintaining code quality was the leading goal for the policy.

Among quality concerns, correctness and subtle bugs came first at 39%. Copyright and licensing issues concerned 75% of respondents.

Figure omitted — see the original article

For AI-generated documentation, 65% would accept it with human review. Some 54% supported limited use of AI tools in project infrastructure, while 29% opposed it.

The survey informed the creation of an AI working group with members holding a range of views. It held its kickoff meeting on October 7 and plans a final report in Q4.

The policy debate is already affecting concrete work.

The Q3 report's entry on NFS over RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) says generative AI produced the server-side code. Testing of the client side is going well, and it is expected to reach FreeBSD's main branch within weeks. The project cannot officially merge the server code while it lacks an AI policy, so the code is available as an unofficial port that builds a kernel module.

The lack of a policy prevents an official merge, which creates a practical reason to write one. The code arrived before the rules for accepting it.

While FreeBSD debates how to accept AI contributions, scrapers collecting data for AI companies continue to attack its infrastructure.

The Cluster Administration Team reports that scrapers collecting LLM training data are attacking FreeBSD.org infrastructure constantly. Scraping has shifted from company infrastructure to botnets using residential proxies, which route traffic through household and business networks. This makes scraper traffic hard to distinguish from legitimate requests. The team says blocking it at the network edge risks substantial collateral damage.

The main target is cgit.FreeBSD.org, the web interface for FreeBSD source code. The report calls the scrapers targeting it "trainers of probabilistic malware." Traffic arrives continuously from compromised devices around the world.

During Q3, the Cluster Administration Team deployed additional cgit mirrors in California and Paris to spread the load. It reported spending considerable time mitigating distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks that quarter.

The Bugmeister Team also lists this as its highest priority. It says the cause is known and the Core Team recognizes the severity, but Bugmeister has limited means to address it.

A volunteer operations team defends a cluster with 143 physical machines and 324 jails, for 467 installations across 14 sites. The traffic comes at botnet scale. The resources on each side remain uneven.

Another source of pressure is the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). Vulnerability and incident reporting requirements for manufacturers took effect on September 11, 2026. Reporting requirements for open-source software stewards begin on December 11, 2027.

The FreeBSD Core Team published a statement recognizing the FreeBSD Foundation as the project's open-source software steward. The foundation has prepared a cybersecurity policy and CRA reporting protocol and published guidance for business users and community members on its website.

A framework that automatically generates software bills of materials (SBOMs) at build time has entered review. An amd64 build produces 218 artifacts, with one for each base package and each library actually used in the build, enabling the full dependency chain to be traced. It supports SPDX 2.2 and Lite 3.0.1 output, with CycloneDX support underway. SBOM support for the ports tree is undergoing separate review.

The security team itself has started using AI in its work. Pierre Pronchery, a security engineer with the Linux Foundation's Alpha-Omega project, demonstrated a CI/CD workflow integrating a self-hosted LLM into a staging instance of Forgejo. It automates draft replies to vulnerability reports, analysis, advisory template preparation, compliance checks, signing, and uploads. The LLM is self-hosted to preserve confidentiality, and the workflow can be useful in production without the LLM.

A policy for code contributions is still in development, while AI has already entered security workflow automation. Here too, practice has moved ahead of policy.

FreeBSD is also becoming easier to use as a desktop OS.

Work continues on a script for the bsdinstall(8) installer that automatically configures a desktop environment. The script has shrunk from about 400 lines in Q1 to about 100. Four new ports, totaling 26 packages, cover automatic setup of GPU drivers, the KDE desktop, and the display manager. They have been submitted to Bugzilla.

A new bsddialog version adds accessibility themes including high contrast, one that avoids red, and one that avoids yellow and blue. Themes can now be managed centrally through system-wide or per-user configuration files. The team also acquired a HumanWare BrailleNote Apex and successfully tested it with FreeBSD. It could display text on the braille display and receive input from the braille keyboard over USB.

Suspend and resume work includes support for S0ix, a low-power sleep state used by recent Intel and AMD laptops. More models lack traditional ACPI S3 sleep support. Thunderbolt controllers can now resume as well.

On AWS EC2, a new desktop AMI for FreeBSD 15 provides a KDE environment accessible through xrdp.

Across Q3, the FreeBSD Foundation sponsored 530 commits to src, which covers the kernel and userland, 82 to ports, and 19 to doc. FreeBSD 14.5-RELEASE shipped in September, and 15.2-RELEASE is scheduled for December. The port of AMD's ROCm GPU computing platform also advanced: the amdkfd driver compiled, linked, and loaded, exposing /dev/kfd. The Bhyve VM management GUI, Bhyvemgr, moved to a client-server architecture. The foundation expanded its support for the Sylve web management platform through a new grant.

The 51 reports show how one project can use AI, prepare for rules around it, and defend against AI-related attacks at the same time. What policy will the FreeBSD working group produce in Q4? Alongside the answers from GCC, QEMU, and Debian, the open-source community is waiting for FreeBSD's.

Originally published on Joho no Todai. The Japanese original is here.

#9650. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9648. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9647. Building a Real-Time Fisheye Camera on iOS 27: Metal, Core Image & Core Graphics

Ever wondered what it takes under the hood to render a real-time 90s skate-style fisheye lens on an iPhone—without dropping a single frame? 🛹📱

I recently took WarpyCam app for a spin on iOS 27 to test its ultra-wide lens distortion in real-world street and portrait conditions. Ditching bulky clip-on hardware for software optics is great as a photographer, but watching a live camera feed warp smoothly at high frame rates immediately got my iOS Developer brain thinking about the graphics pipeline making it possible.

Here is the hands-on test footage first, followed by a breakdown of how Apple's graphics stack powers apps like this:

Building a zero-latency fisheye camera app on iOS isn't just about applying a static post-processing filter. When processing live AVFoundation camera buffers (CMSampleBuffer / CVPixelBuffer), every millisecond counts. Pull it off cleanly, and you have to balance three core Apple frameworks:

Real-time optical distortion requires remapping UV pixel coordinates across every incoming camera frame at 60–120 fps.

Lens geometry is only half of the 90s skate-video aesthetic. Nailing that authentic retro look relies on subtle chromatic aberration, film grain, vignette, and color grading.

While Metal and Core Image handle the heavy pixel-level lifting, Core Graphics (CGContext) shines when dealing with vector precision and final image composition:

Seeing apps push native iOS 27 camera capabilities like this is always inspiring—especially when complex GPU engineering stays completely invisible to the person behind the shutter.

Over to you, fellow iOS & graphics devs: When building real-time camera filters, do you prefer writing custom Metal shaders from scratch for maximum control, or leaning on Core Image filter chains for faster iteration? Drop your thoughts (and favorite shader tricks) in the comments! 👇

#9645. Beyond Fiber Optics: The Hardware Reality of a Decentralized Internet

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

In its 2023 report, the digital rights group Access Now documented 283 internet shutdowns across 39 countries. While this figure includes targeted platform blocking rather than just total national blackouts, it highlights a stark reality: various state actors and conflicting parties hold the ultimate trump card. They can simply issue administrative orders to local telecom operators to restrict routing or suspend connectivity.

Web3 developers have spent years bulletproofing consensus mechanisms and peer-to-peer storage. Yet, if the physical fiber-optic cables belong to a state monopoly, software encryption cannot protect network availability. Furthermore, even when physical lines remain active, governments can compel ISPs to execute software-level blocks like SNI (Server Name Indication) filtering. Whether through severing physical connections or enforcing digital filters at the ISP level, access to even the most decentralized dApp becomes severely restricted for average users.

This physical bottleneck highlights the core motivation behind Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePIN). Projects in the satellite space, including Spacecoin, are engineering architectures to decouple network access from terrestrial telecoms. However, bypassing legacy ISPs is not an absolute cure for censorship—it merely shifts the battleground from software firewalls to hardware logistics.

Many assume that orbital networks bypass terrestrial laws entirely, but Starlink’s recent legal battle in Brazil illustrates the limitations of centralized physical infrastructure.

After the Brazilian Supreme Court ordered X (formerly Twitter) blocked, Starlink initially refused to comply. After Justice Alexandre de Moraes froze Starlink's local accounts over potential liability for fines owed by X, Starlink notified the telecom regulator that it would comply with the court's blocking order. While Starlink publicly maintained that the asset freeze was illegal, this chronological sequence of events underscores how operating as a centralized corporate entity with a vulnerable financial footprint creates distinct compliance chokepoints.

Web3 infrastructure projects aim to solve this by separating the coordination protocol from physical data routing. However, it is crucial to distinguish between protocol decentralization and physical hardware ownership. According to deployment updates, Spacecoin's CTC-0 nanosatellite launched in December 2024, followed by three CTC-1 satellites in November 2025. These satellites are physically owned and operated by a traditional corporate entity (Space Telecommunications Inc.).

The Spacecoin protocol does not decentralize the physical satellite ownership. Instead, its technical roadmap outlines a separation of capabilities. According to Spacecoin's official updates, its protocol is designed to manage authorization, authentication, and accounting across the decentralized infrastructure, while smart contracts and crypto payments support bandwidth coordination. However, the extent to which these capabilities are operational in the deployed satellite network remains distinct from the protocol's stated design.

On October 1, 2025, Spacecoin claimed a successful demonstration using its CTC-0 satellite to transmit secured data over 7,000 kilometers between Chile and the Azores. While Spacecoin has since announced regional connectivity pilots and commercial partnerships in 2026, a globally resilient, independently accessible satellite internet service remains a different milestone from its initial proofs of concept.

Treating orbital networks as an instant bypass for censorship ignores how physical infrastructure is regulated. Moving the internet to an orbital mesh introduces distinct vectors for state control.

Space is borderless, but RF (Radio Frequency) spectrum is strictly policed. Transmitting high-speed data to orbit typically involves licensed spectrum, such as Ku, Ka, L, or S bands. Legally utilizing these frequencies requires two distinct regulatory processes: international coordination through the ITU for frequency assignments and orbital positions—including procedures intended to prevent harmful interference—and separate national authorizations granted by local communications regulators within their jurisdictions. If a decentralized project operates outside authorized spectrum allocations or exceeds the technical limits applicable to license-exempt ISM bands, state actors may treat the transmissions as unlawful. Governments do not necessarily need to attack the blockchain; they can confiscate unauthorized hardware or, in specific scenarios, attempt to deploy localized radio jamming equipment to disrupt targeted frequencies.

While downloading data via a passive receiver can sometimes go unnoticed, two-way satellite internet requires user terminals to transmit data back to orbit. These uplink transmissions emit RF signatures that, with specialized equipment, can potentially be detected and localized. Regimes can outlaw the import and possession of unauthorized satellite terminals. If customs agencies seize the hardware at the border, it can severely restrict network deployment before a single node comes online.

Launching nanosatellites and manufacturing custom RF receivers requires massive upfront capital. If a decentralized network relies on a small number of aerospace launch providers or hardware manufacturers to deploy its infrastructure, those companies become the new chokepoints. A state actor merely needs to apply regulatory pressure on the hardware manufacturers or impose import restrictions to cripple the network's expansion.

Decentralized physical infrastructure does not erase state control. Instead, it forces a shift in the logistics of executing it.

Today, restricting internet access is a relatively straightforward administrative task that relies on legal mandates enforced through local regulators, government agencies, and compliant telecom operators. Censoring a blockchain-coordinated satellite network, however, expands the required enforcement toolkit. It creates a scenario where a state might be forced to strictly police domestic hardware supply chains and import channels, actively track localized RF uplinks, or seize physical terminals.

A decentralized physical internet does not stop governments from using inexpensive software blocks; rather, it introduces a reality where regimes may have to supplement digital firewalls with highly visible, financially exhausting physical enforcement.
